newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO hails U.S.-Russia summit outcome.
newsitem.headline: NATO hails U.S.-Russia summit outcome.

text.p: NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, who is mandated with negotiating a NATO-Russia pact, hailed on Friday the U.S.-Russia summit as a major step forward in developing a more secure and peaceful Europe.
An official statement issued by NATO said Solana was "especially encouraged" by Russian President Boris Yeltsin's commitment to conclude a deal with the Alliance in the near future.
"The secretary general welcomes the many positive results of the Helsinki summit," the statement said without giving any details of what particular aspect of the meeting it found most satisfying.
Solana, who is negotiating the pact to go hand in hand with the Alliance's eastwards expansion, is due to meet Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov for more talks next month.

NATO officials said that, although there was no deal on enlargement at the U.S.-Russia summit in Helsinki on Friday, it appeared Yeltsin had been assured his country would not be left out of a new post-Cold War security order.
"No one expected a deal, and we must wait for details, but it appears the summit has met our best expectations," said one senior alliance official.
U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Strobe Talbott, Washington's main point man on Russia, is due to brief NATO's 16 ambassadors in detail on the summit at a special meeting in Brussels on Saturday.
"The overall climate looked good, and it seems there has been progress across the field," added the official.
He said Clinton's number one objective -- to convince Yeltsin NATO was not hostile and Russia would not be left out of an emerging post-Cold War European security order -- had been met.

Other alliance officials said Yeltsin had appeared relaxed and had made an important concession in agreeing that any final NATO-Russia document should not take the form of a legal treaty, but could be endorsed by alliance heads of government.
NATO has said it wants a "politically binding" document because it would be more flexible and would take far less time to agree than if it had to pass through every NATO member state's parliament.
